chunks.text: 45-year-old male, Associate Professional or Technician, resident of Bedok, Singapore.
Fractured right wrist (15 years ago, fully healed)
General Anesthesia with Ultrasound-Guided Regional Anesthesia (TAP Block) for Post-Operative Pain Management

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: Good morning, Mr./Ms. [Patient's Name]. I'm [Provider's Name], the anesthesiologist who will be taking care of you during your surgery today. I'd like to go through a few questions to ensure we have all the necessary information for your safety and comfort.

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: Good morning, Doctor. I'm ready when you are.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: Thank you. Can you please confirm for me the reason for your surgery today and how long you've been experiencing symptoms?

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: Yes, sure. I've been having a lot of pain on my right side, especially after eating. The doctor said it's due to gallstones and that the best option is to remove the gallbladder laparoscopically.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: Thank you for sharing that. Now, let's move on to your medications. Can you confirm your current list of medications, including any changes or discontinuations in the past year, and any new allergies or reactions since your last medical review?

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: Okay, let me think. I'm still taking Metformin 500mg twice a day for my diabetes, Lisinopril 10mg once a day for blood pressure, and Atorvastatin 20mg at night for cholesterol. Oh, and I stopped taking Ranitidine about six months ago because my acid reflux got better, so now I'm taking Omeprazole 20mg once a day instead.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: Thank you for that update. It's important we have the most current information. Regarding allergies, you mentioned Penicillin causing a rash in the past. Have you had any new allergies or reactions to any medications, foods, or latex since your last review?

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: No, Doctor. Just the Penicillin rash. Nothing new has come up.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: Great, thank you. Now, in terms of your general health, can you tell me about your daily activities and any limitations you might have due to your obesity, diabetes, or hypertension?

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: Well, I do find it harder to move around because of my weight, and sometimes I get short of breath. But I can still do most daily tasks, just slower. My diabetes and blood pressure are managed with medication, and I check my sugar levels regularly.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: Thank you for sharing that. It helps us understand how to support you better during and after surgery. Have you had any previous surgeries or anesthesia? If so, were there any issues?

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: Yes, I had a cesarean section about 10 years ago, and that went smoothly. No issues with the anesthesia that I remember.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: Excellent. And finally, can you confirm when you last had food and drink? It's important for your safety under general anesthesia.

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: I had my last meal around 8 PM last night and a sip of water at 10 PM. Nothing since then, as per the instructions.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: Perfect, thank you. We'll be using general anesthesia for your laparoscopic cholecystectomy and also performing an ultrasound-guided TAP block for post-operative pain management. This should help keep you comfortable after surgery.

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: That sounds good. I'm hoping the pain won't be too bad after.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: We'll do our best to manage your pain effectively. If you have any questions or concerns before we proceed, please let me know.

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: No, I think that's all. Thank you, Doctor.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: You're very welcome. We'll take good care of you. I'll see you in the operating room shortly.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: [08:00] induction propofol one hundred twenty milligrams

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: [08:05] tube in, grade one view

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: [08:10] 18 gauge peripheral line placed, 500 ml lactated ringers bolus

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: [08:15] ultrasound-guided TAP block performed with 0.5% bupivacaine twenty milligrams

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: [08:30] blood pressure drop to eighty over fifty, atropine one milligram given

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: [09:00] surgery completed, reversal with neostigmine two milligrams and sugammadex fifty milligrams

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: Hi there, how are you feeling now after the surgery?

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: I'm okay, I guess. Still a bit groggy, but the pain isn't too bad.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: Good to hear. Can you tell me your pain level out of 10?

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: Maybe a 3 or 4? It's more like discomfort than sharp pain.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: That's expected with the TAP block still working. Are you feeling nauseous at all?

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: No, not really. A bit thirsty, but no nausea.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: Great. How's your breathing? Any tightness or difficulty breathing?

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: No, I'm breathing fine. Just a bit tired from the anesthesia, I think.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: Good. Do you remember anything from the operating room?

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: Not really. I went to sleep and woke up here, so I think I was out completely.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: That's normal under general anesthesia. Given your diabetes and high blood pressure, we'll keep a close eye on your vitals and sugar levels. Any concerns from your side?

segments.speaker: PATIENT
segments.text: No, everything seems fine. Just want to go home and rest.

segments.speaker: PROVIDER
segments.text: We'll get you ready for that soon. Let the nurse know if the pain increases or if you feel unwell in any way.

45-year-old male undergoing elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy under general anesthesia with TAP block for post-operative pain management. Patient has well-controlled but active comorbidities including diabetes, hypertension, and obesity (ASA-PS Class III).

Patient's current medications include Metformin 500 mg twice daily, Lisinopril 10 mg once daily, and Atorvastatin 20 mg once daily. Omeprazole 20 mg once daily was started 6 months ago, and Ranitidine was discontinued at the same time. No known drug allergies, but reports a history of penicillin rash.

Past medical history includes resolved pneumonia 5 years ago, fully healed right wrist fracture 15 years ago, and resolved hypothyroidism 8 years ago. No recent respiratory issues, no recurrence of hypothyroidism, and no history of adverse reactions to anesthetics or medications.
Patient last ate at 8 PM and had a sip of water at 10 PM. No history of heart disease or uncontrolled hypertension.

Intraoperative course included propofol induction, endotracheal intubation with grade one view, peripheral line placement, lactated ringers bolus, and TAP block with bupivacaine. Transient hypotension (80/50) occurred and was treated with atropine. Surgery completed without further complications.
Reversal of neuromuscular blockade was achieved with neostigmine and sugammadex.
Monitor for post-operative nausea and vomiting (PONV) due to laparoscopic surgery and potential opioid use.
Maintain vigilance for airway complications due to patient's obesity and potential for difficult airway management.
Ensure glycemic control considering the patient's diabetes and the stress response to surgery.
Manage analgesia carefully, balancing the effect of the TAP block with potential opioid requirements.
Monitor hemodynamics closely given the history of hypertension and intraoperative hypotension.
Watch for signs of residual neuromuscular blockade following sugammadex reversal.
